opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a decision we made lightly. We looked at a few paths before coming to that conclusion.

When vLLM started, it was a research project in an academic lab. That works well early on: you have smart students, some compute from sponsors, and the freedom to experiment. But as the project grew and became something a lot of companies run in production, the demands changed. People needed fast bug fixes, support for every new model architecture the day it's released, support for many kinds of hardware, careful performance work, and long-term maintenance. That isn't something you can sustain on PhD students' spare time and a few grants.

So we asked who could support it. One option was for a single big company to take it in-house. But then it risks becoming that company's project. Other companies become hesitant to contribute, and the neutrality that made vLLM a shared piece of infrastructure starts to erode. Another option was relying purely on donations or a foundation. Foundations are great for governance, but in practice they don't fund a full-time team of strong engineers working on a fast-moving, very technical system. The money and the urgency just don't match.

A company lets you do a few things at once. You can hire people full time and pay them competitively, because the talent we need is the same talent every AI lab is trying to hire. You can raise capital that matches the scale of the problem. And if you design it right, you can stay committed to the open-source project being open and neutral, while the company builds value around it, through services, enterprise support, or products built on top of it.

So when I say it felt like the only option, I mean that if we wanted vLLM to stay independent and keep up with how quickly the field is moving, we needed a sustainable organization behind it. A company was the structure that could provide that. The hard part, and what we think about every day, is keeping the open-source project healthy and community-driven while the company exists alongside it.

r001.rationale: The response says a single company might make vLLM seem like that company’s project and erode neutrality, but it does not explain that the company’s existing business commitments make senior management less likely to fully support open-source development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that I woke up one day and decided I wanted to be an entrepreneur. It was more that every other path kept closing off, and starting a company was what was left.

Let me explain the situation. vLLM is a very widely used open-source inference engine. If you look at how large models are actually served today, a huge fraction of that traffic goes through vLLM. But the project has a kind of structural problem: the usage is enormous, and the maintenance burden is enormous, while the people doing the maintenance are a small group, many of them students or volunteers. Every day there are hundreds of issues, dozens of pull requests, new models coming out that users expect support for on day one, new hardware from NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Amazon, all needing adaptation. That workload does not shrink. It grows with the ecosystem.

So the question becomes, who pays for this? Open source itself doesn't generate revenue. The traditional answer is a foundation or a university lab. But a university can only support a few PhD students, and PhD students have to graduate. They need papers, not merge requests. A foundation can hold the trademark and governance, but it doesn't usually fund dozens of full-time engineers. Donations help, but they are not predictable, and you can't build a team on something that might disappear next quarter.

The other option is joining a big company and maintaining the project from the inside. I thought seriously about that. The problem is that a big company has its own priorities. If vLLM's roadmap conflicts with the company's product, the company wins. And the community senses that very quickly. Once people believe the project is just one vendor's tool, contributors from other companies pull back, and that's how a neutral open-source project slowly dies. I've seen this happen to other projects. I didn't want vLLM to go that way.

So when I lined up the options, the one that actually worked was to build a company whose business depends on vLLM being healthy and neutral, and then use the company's revenue to pay full-time engineers to work on the open-source project. The commercial side gives us stability. The open-source side gives us the ecosystem and the trust. The two support each other. If the company succeeds, vLLM gets more maintainers. If vLLM thrives, the company has a stronger foundation to build on.

I'll be honest that there's tension in that model. You always have to be careful that the commercial interests don't start pulling the open-source roadmap in a direction the community doesn't want. We think about that constantly. But compared to the alternatives, which were either slowly burning out a handful of volunteers or handing the project to a single large company, this felt like the one option that could keep vLLM alive and independent in the long run. That's why I say it was the only option, not just one option among many.

r001.rationale: The response says a large company may prioritize its own product over vLLM, but does not explain that existing business commitments make it difficult to secure senior management’s commitment to fully support vLLM’s open-source development.

astra-6.text:
The way I saw it, vLLM needed sustained, full-time work. You can build something useful as a research project, but maintaining it is a different commitment: fixing bugs, reviewing contributions, and keeping up with what users need. That work doesn’t necessarily turn into a paper, so it’s difficult to support through academic incentives alone.

Starting a company was a way to make that commitment sustainable—to build a team whose everyday work could support the project. It wasn’t that a company was the only possible way to support open source, but it felt like the path where we could take responsibility for vLLM over the long term.

r001.rationale: The candidate says founding a company could sustain a team’s work on vLLM, but does not explain how a company’s existing business commitments make it difficult to secure senior management’s support for open-source development.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was about making the work sustainable. An open-source project like vLLM needs ongoing engineering: fixing bugs, reviewing contributions, supporting users, and keeping up with new hardware and models. You also need compute to test those changes. That’s difficult to sustain on people’s spare time alone.

I saw starting a company as a way to build a team whose full-time work could support the project, with a business that could pay for that work. I wouldn’t say a company is the only possible way to support open source, but it felt like the path where I could take responsibility for making it sustainable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a company could fund a full-time team, but does not explain that existing business commitments make it difficult to secure senior management’s commitment to vLLM’s open-source development.
